issues.legal_issue: Findings in an earlier final judgment between the same parties remain binding in later proceedings when special leave to appeal from that judgment was not granted.
material_facts: An earlier High Court Division Bench had decided that the government grant was valid, that the claimants were entitled to the price of the land rather than its restoration, and that they had waived their right to occupy it.

The claimants sought special leave to appeal from that judgment, but the Supreme Court disposed of the petition without granting special leave, leaving them liberty to ask the government to consider modifying the grant.
In later proceedings, the High Court treated the earlier findings as non-binding, in part because it considered the earlier judgment per incuriam.
issues.conclusion: The earlier findings remained final and binding between the parties; the Supreme Court's order refusing special leave did not replace or disturb the earlier judgment.
issues.legal_principle: Under Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala, refusal of special leave does not attract the doctrine of merger or substitute the challenged order. A prior judgment's findings between the parties remain binding in later proceedings. The doctrine of per incuriam concerns precedent and does not displace res judicata; as explained in Tarini Charan Bhattacharjee v. Kedar Nath Haldar, the correctness of a prior decision does not determine whether it operates as res judicata.

predicates.earlier_writ_appeal_decided_issues: An earlier appellate proceeding decided issues concerning the same underlying dispute.
predicates.same_parties_later_proceeding: The parties to the earlier proceeding or their successors raised the dispute again in a later proceeding.
predicates.special_leave_not_granted: The reviewing court disposed of the challenge without granting special leave to appeal.

issues.definition: When the same parties relitigate issues decided in an earlier appellate proceeding and special leave was not granted, the earlier decisions on those issues remain binding.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge to a government grant cannot be raised in later proceedings on a ground that was available but omitted from an earlier challenge to the same grant.
material_facts: The claimants had earlier challenged the government grant in court.
They did not raise in that challenge the contention that restrictions on acquiring, holding, or transferring agricultural land invalidated the grant for house sites.
They later relied on that contention to challenge the same grant.
issues.conclusion: The omitted ground could not be raised in the later proceeding because of constructive res judicata.
issues.legal_principle: Explanation IV to Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure embodies constructive res judicata and applies to writ proceedings. It bars a matter that might and ought to have been raised in the earlier proceeding. The Court relied on Direct Recruit Class II Engineering Officers' Association v. State of Maharashtra and Forward Construction Co. v. Prabhat Mandal. A fresh cause of action may support a new proceeding, but it does not permit reopening issues or grounds barred by res judicata or constructive res judicata.

predicates.later_challenge_to_same_grant: A claimant challenged the same government grant in a later proceeding.
predicates.earlier_challenge_to_grant: The claimant had previously brought a proceeding challenging that grant.
predicates.available_ground_omitted: The claimant could have raised a ground in the earlier proceeding but did not do so.

issues.definition: A ground that could have been raised in an earlier challenge to a grant is barred when the same claimant raises it in a later challenge to that grant.

issues.legal_issue: A grant of agricultural land for house sites is not invalid merely because statutory restrictions concern agricultural land when the governing land-revenue framework permits conversion to another use on payment of a conversion fine.
material_facts: The government granted land to an association for house sites and made the grant subject to payment of a conversion fine.
The claimants argued that restrictions on acquiring, holding, and transferring agricultural land made the grant void.
The relevant land-revenue provisions permitted agricultural land to be diverted to other purposes on payment of a fine, and the land-grant rules provided for grants of building sites.
issues.conclusion: The grant was not void ab initio on the ground that the agricultural-land restrictions prohibited the grant for house sites.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 79-A, 79-B and 80 of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act concern agricultural lands and must be read with Section 95 of the Karnataka Land Revenue Act, which permits diversion of agricultural land to other uses on payment of a fine. The Court also relied on Rule 18 of the Karnataka Land Grants Rules, 1969, which provides for grants of building sites, and the principle that related statutes concerning the same subject matter are read together.

predicates.challenge_to_grant_for_building_sites: A party challenged a government grant of land intended for building sites.
predicates.land_subject_to_conversion: The granted land was agricultural land capable of being diverted to another use under the applicable land framework.
predicates.conversion_fine_required_for_nonagricult: The governing framework required a fine for converting agricultural land to a non-agricultural use, and the grant was made subject to that requirement.

issues.definition: Where a grant concerns building sites on convertible agricultural land and the applicable framework requires a conversion fine, agricultural-land restrictions alone do not invalidate the grant.

issues.legal_issue: The government cannot use a later administrative decision to reopen issues conclusively decided in a prior judgment between the parties.
material_facts: The earlier High Court judgment had held that the grant was valid, that the claimants were entitled to the price rather than restoration of the land, and that they had waived their right to occupy it.
The Supreme Court later allowed the claimants to apply to the government for modification of the grant but did not direct the government to cancel it.

When considering the application, the government proceeded on the basis that confirmation of the claimants' occupancy rights made them owners and ordered cancellation of the grant and transfer of vacant sites or payment of compensation.
issues.conclusion: The government could consider the application but could not disregard the earlier binding findings; the directions cancelling the grant and transferring vacant sites or awarding compensation were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: A new cause of action may permit a fresh proceeding, but issues already decided between the parties cannot be reopened. The Court relied on State of Haryana v. M.P. Mohla for that distinction and Madan Mohan Pathak v. Union of India for the principle that a final judgment must be obeyed while it stands and cannot be ignored by an executive decision. The Supreme Court's earlier order granted liberty to seek modification but did not mandate cancellation of the grant.

predicates.administrative_reconsideration_after_fin: A government authority reconsidered a matter after a final judgment concerning it.
predicates.prior_judgment_decided_the_dispute: The final judgment decided the parties' rights concerning the disputed grant or property.
predicates.administrative_order_reopens_decided_iss: The authority issued an order based on a position inconsistent with an issue decided in that judgment.

issues.definition: When the government reconsiders a matter after a final judgment has decided the parties' rights, it cannot issue an order that reopens an issue resolved by that judgment.

issues.legal_issue: A government authority cannot transfer public sites held by a development authority or require that authority to acquire its own road land and compensate former claimants without legal authority.
material_facts: The development authority sanctioned the layout subject to roads, civic amenity sites, parks, and utility connections vesting in it without compensation.
The civic amenity sites and road land formed part of the land granted to the association and were included in the sanctioned layout.
The government later directed that vacant civic amenity sites be handed to the claimants and that the development authority acquire the land used for a road and pay compensation to them.
issues.conclusion: The directions to transfer the civic amenity sites and to acquire the road land and pay compensation were without authority of law and were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32(5) of the Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1976 permits the authority to require transfer of layout roads and open spaces without compensation. Section 38-A restricts disposition of areas reserved for parks, playgrounds, and civic amenities, and Section 65 does not authorize government directions contrary to the Act's purposes. The Court relied on Bangalore Medical Trust v. B.S. Muddappa and Bangalore Development Authority v. R. Hanumaiah.

predicates.development_authority_sanctioned_layout: A development authority sanctioned a layout containing roads and public amenity areas.
predicates.public_sites_and_roads_vested_in_authori: The layout conditions provided for the roads and public amenity areas to vest in the development authority without compensation.
predicates.government_order_directed_transfer_or_ac: A government order directed that those areas be transferred to claimants or that the authority acquire road land and compensate them.

issues.definition: When layout conditions vest public sites and roads in a development authority, a government order directing their transfer to claimants or their acquisition for compensation exceeds the authority available under the governing framework.

issues.legal_issue: When courts reject an application for interim relief and a related appeal because the underlying dispute is pending before the Supreme Court, they must reconsider the application and suit after the Supreme Court resolves that dispute.
material_facts: A civil court rejected an application for temporary injunction on the ground that the underlying dispute was pending before the Supreme Court and that the Supreme Court alone should consider interim relief.
The High Court dismissed an appeal from that order because the suit concerned the same subject matter as the Supreme Court proceedings.
The Supreme Court then decided the underlying dispute in connected appeals.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court set aside the orders refusing interim relief and remanded the matter to the civil court to hear the parties and decide the injunction application and suit consistently with its judgment.
issues.legal_principle: Once the Supreme Court has resolved the dispute that was the basis for deferring consideration of interim relief, the pending application and suit should be determined by the trial court in accordance with the Supreme Court's judgment. No earlier case or statutory provision was cited for this disposition.

predicates.civil_suit_seeks_interim_relief: A party brought a civil suit and sought interim relief in that suit.
predicates.lower_courts_deferred_decision_because_s: The lower courts declined to decide the interim application because the underlying dispute was pending before the Supreme Court.
predicates.supreme_court_has_resolved_underlying_di: The Supreme Court subsequently decided the underlying dispute.

issues.definition: If lower courts defer a suit's interim application because the underlying dispute is pending before the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court later decides that dispute, the application and suit are remanded for decision consistent with that judgment.
